about: Rules for the Live a life tab (views/atlas/lenses/life.js). Every number here is a rough, sourced default meant to keep the game honest, not a precise model. Money is counted in day-wages (what an unskilled labourer earned in a day where you are), so a life in Han China and one in Victorian London compare.

src.cite: Scheidel and Meeks, ORBIS: The Stanford Geospatial Network Model of the Roman World (2012): foot travel 30 km a day
ORBIS: horseback 56 km a day; ridden horses spread across the steppe by about 1000 BCE (Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel and Language, 2007)
Bulliet, The Camel and the Wheel (1975): caravans made about 3 to 4 km an hour for 8 to 10 hours a day; domestic camels in Arabian caravan trade by about 1000 BCE
ORBIS models river travel at roughly 1 to 3 km an hour upstream and faster downstream; this game uses one average for both directions
Casson, 'Speed under Sail of Ancient Ships', TAPA 82 (1951): 4 to 6 knots with a fair wind, 2 to 2.5 against; about 100 km a day averaged over a voyage
Bowen, The Business of Empire (2006): East India Company ships took about five to six months from England to India around the Cape
Headrick, The Tentacles of Progress (1988): by the 1870s steamers via Suez reached Bombay from London in about a month
Wolmar, Blood, Iron and Gold: How the Railways Transformed the World (2009); opening years per region in rail_regions
Rough figure for paved and unpaved inter-city roads of the mid twentieth century
Fares in day-wages fall roughly tenfold from 1950 to 2000 (IATA; Our World in Data, air transport)

Relative speeds are the game's own rough weights, in the spirit of ORBIS's terrain costs and Naismith's rule (W. W. Naismith, 1892: an extra hour for every 600 m climbed); deserts are slow on foot and fine by camel (Bulliet 1975)

seasons.why: Roman and medieval sailors kept off the Mediterranean from mid-November to mid-March: short days, cloud that hid the stars, and winter gales.

src.cite: Vegetius, Epitoma rei militaris 4.39; Casson, Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World (1971)

seasons.heading: east
seasons.why: From April to September the monsoon blows from the south-west: ships from Arabia and Africa run fast to India, and nothing sails the other way.

src.cite: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea 57 (1st century CE); Hourani, Arab Seafaring in the Indian Ocean (1951, rev. 1995)

seasons.heading: west
seasons.why: From November to March the wind turns: ships from India run home to Arabia and East Africa.

src.cite: Hourani, Arab Seafaring in the Indian Ocean (1951, rev. 1995)

seasons.heading: north
seasons.why: Junks sailed north to China on the summer monsoon and south to the Straits on the winter one, so traders waited months at Malacca or Quanzhou.

src.cite: Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce 1450-1680, vol. 2 (1993)

seasons.heading: south
seasons.why: The winter monsoon carried junks south from China to the Straits of Malacca and Java.

src.cite: Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce 1450-1680, vol. 2 (1993)

seasons.why: The Baltic and White Seas freeze or close in winter; the Hansa laid up its ships from November to February.

src.cite: Dollinger, The German Hansa (1970)

seasons.why: High passes like the Alps, the Hindu Kush and the Pamirs closed or turned deadly under winter snow.

src.cite: Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History (2012); Xuanzang's own account of losing men to snow and cold crossing the Tian Shan (Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, 646)

seasons.why: Spring thaw and autumn rain turned Russian and Ukrainian roads to mud; travel waited for the ground to freeze or dry.

src.cite: Rasputitsa (Wikipedia)

seasons.why: Once rivers froze, sledges ran on the ice and snow faster than carts ever did in summer.

src.cite: Winter road (Wikipedia): sledge roads on frozen rivers

seasons.why: Caravans moved at night or waited out the summer heat; the great Sahara crossings left in autumn and winter.

src.cite: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (Sijilmasa to Walata, 1352): the caravan left in February

seasons.why: Monsoon and summer rains flooded tropical tracks and rivers; armies and traders waited for the dry season.

src.cite: Gommans, Mughal Warfare (2002): campaigning seasons and the monsoon

ports.why: You can only board a ship at a port. Waiting for a sailing and a berth usually took days; finding a boat on an empty coast took weeks.

roads.why: Paved roads with milestones and way-stations (the cursus publicus) across the Roman world.

src.cite: ORBIS; Chevallier, Roman Roads (1976)

roads.why: Herodotus counts 111 way-stations on the road from Sardis to Susa.

src.cite: Herodotus, Histories 5.52-53

roads.why: The Qhapaq Nan, some 30,000 km of road with tambo rest-houses, crossing the Andes.

src.cite: Hyslop, The Inka Road System (1984)

roads.why: Relay stations every 30 to 50 km let official travellers with a paiza pass ride across Eurasia.

src.cite: Silverstein, Postal Systems in the Pre-Modern Islamic World (2007), ch. 4 on the Mongol yam

roads.why: Along a working trade route you travel with caravans, find inns and wells, and are safer.

src.cite: Trade routes from the Atlas economy-trade workstream (data/economy-trade/routes.jsonl)

hazards.why: Travellers died of disease, exposure, shipwreck and bandits; these rates are rough guesses, set below the several percent of people aboard who died on a typical Dutch East India Company voyage to Asia (Bruijn, Gaastra and Schoffer, Dutch-Asiatic Shipping, 1987).

src.cite: Bruijn, Gaastra and Schoffer, Dutch-Asiatic Shipping in the 17th and 18th Centuries (1987)

life_table.about: Gompertz-Makeham hazard h(age) = A + B*exp(G*age) for adults, calibrated to remaining life expectancy at 15 (e15). Before 1800 e15 is set near 31 to 33 years, as in model life tables for populations with life expectancy at birth of 25 to 35; after 1800 it follows the global rise.

src.cite: Coale and Demeny, Regional Model Life Tables and Stable Populations (2nd ed., 1983)
Volk and Atkinson, 'Infant and child death in the human environment of evolutionary adaptation', Evolution and Human Behavior 34 (2013): about half of children died before 15
Riley, 'Estimates of regional and global life expectancy, 1800-2001', Population and Development Review 31 (2005)
Loudon, Death in Childbirth (1992): roughly 1 maternal death per 100 births before modern obstetrics

plague.why: In a town struck by plague a person had roughly a one in three chance of dying in the Black Death and about one in eight in later outbreaks. Those who could fled ('quickly, far, and come back late') and the rich died less.

src.cite: Biraben, Les hommes et la peste en France et dans les pays europeens et mediterraneens (1975-76): the dated outbreak list behind the map
Benedictow, The Black Death 1346-1353: The Complete History (2004)
Alfani, 'Plague in seventeenth-century Europe and the decline of Italy', European Review of Economic History 17 (2013)

famine.why: A famine year raised deaths several times over, mostly through hunger-driven disease.

src.cite: Ó Gráda, Famine: A Short History (2009)
Allen, 'Economic structure and agricultural productivity in Europe, 1300-1800', European Review of Economic History 4 (2000)
ILO modelled estimates via Our World in Data: share of employment in agriculture (1991 44 percent, 2019 27 percent)

roles.what: You work the land, owe rent, tax or labour to someone above you, and live by the harvest.
You follow your animals between pastures; your wealth walks on four legs.
You are a smith, potter, weaver or builder in a town, with a trade you learned as an apprentice.
You buy cheap in one place and sell dear in another; one good voyage can make you, one bad one break you.
You work ships out of your home port for wages and a share of the cargo.
You serve a lord or a state for pay, food and the hope of plunder.
You can read, which few around you can; you serve a temple, church, mosque, court or school.
You were born to land and rank; you live on rents, and politics can kill you.
You work long shifts in a mill, mine or workshop for a weekly wage.
You work with paper: an office, a shop, a school or a government desk.
